title: Sustainability and Inclusion in Museum Shops
content:
Think about the last time you left a museum. You wandered through exhibits showcasing human ingenuity, culture, and history. Then, as you exited, you probably passed by the gift shop. At first glance, it may have seemed like just another place to buy souvenirs, a cute magnet, a tote bag, maybe a book about the exhibits. But what if we told you that this little corner of the museum is actually a microcosm of some of the biggest trends in retail today?

Museum shops can connect a collection with the people and processes behind the things they sell. Choosing suppliers carefully, explaining how products are made and keeping a range affordable can make retail part of a museum’s wider mission. The examples below show different ways to approach that work.

The Jet Engine Turbine Wall Clock offers a useful starting point. In May 2023, the Museum Store Association highlighted the Museum of Flight’s clock, made by The Chicago Lighthouse. The manufacturer’s employment mission is the relevant connection: Chicago Lighthouse Industries provides industrial work for people who are legally blind.

title: Culture Dose for Kids: Art Gallery Programme for Anxious Children
content:
Suppose you were asked to design something to help children with anxiety. You would probably reach for a clinic, a trained therapist and a carefully measured course of treatment. You would almost certainly not reach for an art gallery, a sketchbook and a cup of tea.

Yet that is roughly what the Art Gallery of New South Wales (AGNSW) and the Black Dog Institute, a mental health research organisation, built together. Culture Dose for Kids (CDK) is an eight-week programme for children aged 9 to 12 with anxiety, and for the parents or guardians who come with them. Each 90-minute session involves looking at just three artworks, making something with no right answer, and talking about it if you feel like it.

When Danielle Gullotta, AGNSW’s Senior Access Programmes Producer, presented the programme at the Museums, Health & Wellbeing Summit 2026, what stood out wasn’t any single activity. It was how many of the programme’s choices run against the instincts most museums have. Look closely and each one turns out to make a strange kind of sense.

title: What Städel learned from designing an art app with people living with dementia
content:
The Städel Museum spent years learning how people living with dementia respond to art in its galleries. Then it had to work out how much of that experience could survive on a screen.

During one testing session for ARTEMIS Digital, a couple sat looking at Max Liebermann’s painting of girls sewing in an Amsterdam orphanage. The wife, who is living with dementia, said nothing about the picture. Instead, her hands began to move, recreating the stitching motions of the girls on the screen.

Anne Dribbisch of the Städel’s art education team shared that moment at MuseumNext, in a presentation with Dr Chantal Eschenfelder, the museum’s Head of Education and Digital Collection. It sums up what the project is after. The aim is not to teach people about art history, but to prompt a response, and to give a person with dementia and the person who cares for them something to share.
